"Win at All Cost" Series Documents Prosecutorial Abuses; Now What? Or So What?

(Marijuananews note: The Pittsburgh Post-Gazette has just completed a 10 part series on prosecutorial abuses that should win a Pulitzer Prize. This is journalism at its finest.

As the editorial below concludes, "The reaction across the nation to the Block News Alliance series strengthens our conviction that prosecutors who bend and even break the law are not an isolated occurrence. If the Justice Department doesn’t act on its own to curb abuses, increase accountability and own up to its injustices, Congress will - and should - step in."

As visitors to this site know, it is my view that we have a major crisis in law enforcement, and many of the worst abuses occur in marijuana cases. However -- or therefore, I am not as optimistic as the Post-Gazette’s editors about Congress doing anything meaningful about these abuses.

If they will prohibit counting a vote, and urge the persecution and/or prosecution of the sick and dying who use medical marijuana, why should they object to framing tens of thousands of innocent people. This is simply the price that they are willing to pay to preserve the system.

One of the least convincing arguments that I have heard for impeaching Clinton is that we must make clear that everyone is equal before the law. Do they really expect us to believe that? No, but they have to say it, just as they have to keep saying that the medical marijuana movement is a plot to "legalize all drugs."

I predict the following: Sometime next year the Justice Department will "look into" the matter, and after a year or two they will either not respond at all, or create a bureaucratic mechanism that appears to address the problem.

After that, someone in Congress will introduce a bill to do something. The Justice Department will ask to study the bill and to make some suggestions "to improve it."

Two to four more years will pass, and then Justice will submit a revised version that actually increases the arbitrary powers of the prosecutors. The original sponsor of the bill will declare himself satisfied and move the bill through Congress.

I am not just being cynical. This is exactly what happened when Representative Henry Hyde complained about and then eventually introduced a bill to limit the abuses of the civil forfeiture laws. Hyde initially accepted a Justice Department version that made matters much worse, before he finally woke up and returned to his original bill, which has gone nowhere. For more information on forfeiture see www.fear.org

Forfeiture, although a major problem, is relatively peripheral to the operation of the system. The abuse of prosecutorial power goes to the very heart of the way law enforcement works. The abuses are so widespread and so deeply ingrained into the system that it will take something that totally discredits the system – such as recognizing that marijuana prohibition is a fraud – to make such reforms possible.

One interesting indicator to watch for – How many other papers around the country will look into prosecutorial abuses in their areas? The local criminal defense bar could provide them with endless examples. Don’t hold your breath.)

EDITORIAL: PROSECUTION OR PERSECUTION?

"The philosophy of the past 10 years [is] that whatever works is all right."

That statement by a former federal prosecutor in Florida pithily sums up "Win at All Costs," Block News Alliance reporter Bill Moushey’s 10-part series on abuse and lawbreaking by prosecutors and federal agents. The question is whether the U.S. Department of Justice has gotten the message.

If it does not move on its own to rein in prosecutors who cross the line between prosecution and persecution, it can expect Congress to step in.

Mr. Moushey and colleague Bob Martinson reported that federal agents and prosecutors broke the law in hundreds of cases. They have offered a wealth of detail amassed in a two-year investigation to suggest that, on the theory that "if it works it’s all right," federal prosecutors and law enforcement agents have:

Not all of the blame lies with the Justice Department and its oblivious overseers. Fighting the "war on drugs" not wisely but too well, Congress has promulgated harsh mandatory minimum sentences for even small-time drug offenders, crowding the prisons and increasing the pressure on defendants facing years in prison to cooperate by implicating others, whether or not their information is true. Congress also has given a green light to sting operations.

The U.S. Supreme Court, meanwhile, has marched in lockstep with Congress in "cracking down" on crime by eviscerating protections for defendants that also served to keep law enforcement honest. Perhaps most egregious was the high court’s decision that the withholding by prosecutors of potentially exculpatory material could be a "harmless error" rather than a factor that would doom a prosecution.

But if Congress and the courts have contributed to a climate in which prosecutors try to "win at any cost," it is the Justice Department and its understaffed Office of Professional Responsibility that deserve the bulk of the blame for the abuses documented by the series.

And while Congress shows signs of recognizing that prosecution too often becomes persecution, the Justice Department shows precious little awareness that many of its operatives are running roughshod over the rights of citizens. We await a significant and sustained response to the series by Attorney General Janet Reno and her lieutenants, but early indications are that the department doesn’t recognize the magnitude of the problem.

Responding to the series, Mary Jo White, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York, pointed out that thousands of federal cases have been pursued without any charge of misconduct. No doubt, but Mr. Moushey’s investigation of 1,500 allegations of abuse suggests that, while wrongdoing occurs in a minority of cases, it is a sizable minority and one that seems to be growing.

Reasonable people can disagree about the precise remedies for these abuses. At the minimum, victims of prosecutorial misconduct should be able to collect significant damages. Complaints to OPR should not be entombed in bureaucratic silence; the agency should provide specific accounts of the disposition of these complaints and whether, and how, the wrongdoers were punished.

And while an independent oversight board for prosecutors might be unwieldy or subject to political pressure, Justice Department officials who oppose the creation of such a body have the burden of demonstrating that they can be trusted to prevent and punish lapses on their own.

The reaction across the nation to the Block News Alliance series strengthens our conviction that prosecutors who bend and even break the law are not an isolated occurrence. If the Justice Department doesn’t act on its own to curb abuses, increase accountability and own up to its injustices, Congress will - and should - step in.
